lessons.title: Sorting Complexity Comparison
lessons.objective: State the time complexity, space complexity, stability, and correct use case for every major sorting algorithm — so you can justify any sorting choice in a design or interview context.
concepts: Comparison-based lower bound: O(n log n) optimal
Bubble sort: O(n²) — educational only
Selection sort: O(n²) — minimal swaps
Insertion sort: O(n²) worst, O(n) best — fast for small/nearly-sorted arrays
Merge sort: O(n log n) stable — guaranteed
Quick sort: O(n log n) average — fast in practice
Heap sort: O(n log n) in-place — no extra space
Counting/bucket/radix: O(n) — bounded domain only
JavaScript Array.sort(): TimSort — stable, O(n log n)
lessons.explanation: Every sorting algorithm makes a tradeoff between time, space, stability, and applicability. Bubble sort and selection sort are O(n²) and serve no production purpose but illustrate the comparison lower bound. Insertion sort is O(n²) worst case but O(n) on nearly-sorted arrays — this is why TimSort uses it for small subarrays, which are often nearly sorted due to natural ordering in real data. Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) in all cases and is stable but uses O(n) extra space. Quicksort averages O(n log n) and is in-place (O(log n) stack) but has O(n²) worst case with bad pivot selection. Heapsort is O(n log n) and in-place with O(1) extra space but is not stable and has poor cache performance. JavaScript's Array.sort() implements TimSort: a hybrid of merge sort (for larger runs) and insertion sort (for small runs), giving guaranteed O(n log n) stable sort. Knowing which algorithm your language uses matters: Python uses TimSort, Java uses dual-pivot quicksort for primitives and TimSort for objects, C++ std::sort is typically an introsort (quicksort + heapsort hybrid).
lessons.analogy: Sorting algorithms are like different ways to tidy a room. Bubble sort is picking up one item, comparing it to every other item, and slowly moving it to its correct place — exhausting. Insertion sort is tidying a pile one card at a time, sliding each card to its correct position in the already-tidy portion — fast when the pile is almost tidy. Merge sort is dividing the room into sections, tidying each section separately, then combining. Quicksort is picking a reference item, putting everything smaller on one side and larger on the other, then tidying each side.

code_example.explanation: The most important row in this table for interviews is Quick Sort. The O(n²) worst case is real but irrelevant with randomised pivot in practice. The O(log n) space from the call stack is the true space complexity — not O(1). Many candidates incorrectly state quicksort is O(1) space; it is O(log n) average and O(n) worst case due to the recursive call stack.

common_mistakes: Stating quicksort is O(1) space — it uses O(log n) average call stack depth with balanced partitions and O(n) worst case with unbalanced; only iterative versions with explicit tail-call optimisation achieve O(log n) space guarantee

Using arr.sort() for numeric sorting without a comparator — JavaScript's default comparator converts elements to strings, so [10,9,2].sort() returns [10,2,9] not [2,9,10]; always provide (a,b) => a-b for numeric sort

Not knowing that Array.sort() in JavaScript is stable since V8 7.0 (Node.js 11+) — before this version it was unstable for arrays longer than 10 elements; modern JavaScript is safe to rely on stability
lessons.interview_relevance: Sorting complexity is a baseline interview topic. 'What sort algorithm would you use and why?' is asked in system design, code review scenarios, and direct algorithm questions. Knowing the full table, being able to justify a choice based on constraints (stability needed, in-place required, bounded domain), and knowing what Array.sort() does internally separates candidates who have thought carefully about algorithms from those who have not.

Candidate: 'I need a stable sort. Merge sort or TimSort. JavaScript Array.sort() uses TimSort which is stable.' Interviewer: 'What if I told you prices are integers 0-10,000?' interview_war_story.lesson: Stability matters when sorting objects by one field while preserving order by another. Always ask: (1) Is the data integers in a bounded range? → counting sort. (2) Are ties meaningful? → stable sort required. (3) Is memory constrained? → heapsort or in-place quicksort.

questions.question: [10,2,9].sort() in JavaScript without a comparator. What does it return?
options: [2,9,10] — numeric sort
[10,2,9] — sorted by string: '10'<'2'<'9' in lexicographic order
An error
questions.explanation: JavaScript's default sort comparator converts elements to strings and sorts lexicographically. '10' < '2' < '9' as strings (character '1' < '2' < '9'). So [10,2,9].sort() = [10,2,9]. Always use .sort((a,b)=>a-b) for numeric arrays. This is one of the most common JavaScript sorting bugs.

questions.question: You need to sort user records by creation timestamp, preserving alphabetical order when timestamps are equal. Which algorithm guarantees correctness?
options: Quicksort — fastest in practice
A stable sort (merge sort, TimSort, stable counting sort) — stability preserves alphabetical order for equal timestamps
Heapsort — in-place
Any sort works — stability does not matter for this problem
questions.explanation: Stability is required: when two records have equal timestamps, the original order (alphabetical) must be preserved. Unstable sorts (quicksort, heapsort) may arbitrarily reorder equal elements. Stable sorts (merge sort, TimSort) guarantee equal elements keep their original relative order. JavaScript's Array.sort() is TimSort (stable since V8 7.0).

questions.question: What is the true space complexity of quicksort (not O(1) as commonly misstated)?
options: O(1) — in-place sorting
O(log n) average (balanced partitions, randomised pivot), O(n) worst case (n-level call stack with unbalanced partitions)
O(n) always
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Quicksort is in-place (no extra arrays) but has a recursive call stack. With balanced partitions: O(log n) call stack depth. With n-1 vs 1 partitions: O(n) call stack. The correct answer is O(log n) average, O(n) worst. Saying O(1) is wrong and a common interview mistake.

theory_mcq.question: Why does insertion sort have a BEST case of O(n) despite a worst case of O(n²), and why does this matter for the lesson's note that it's 'used inside TimSort'?
options: Insertion sort's best and worst cases are actually identical; this distinction is meaningless

Insertion sort's best case occurs on ALREADY (or nearly) SORTED input, where each new element only needs to be compared against its immediate neighbor before being confirmed in place (requiring minimal shifting) — TimSort exploits this by using insertion sort specifically on SMALL or NEARLY-SORTED segments of data (where its O(n) best-case-like behavior shines), while relying on merge-sort-style techniques for the larger overall structure, combining the strengths of both
Insertion sort's best case only applies to arrays containing exactly one element
TimSort never actually uses insertion sort internally; this is a lesson error
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's stated facts: 'Insertion sort: O(n²) worst, O(n) best — fast for small/nearly-sorted arrays' and 'Used inside TimSort' — TimSort (JavaScript's Array.sort()) is a hybrid algorithm that specifically leverages insertion sort's strong performance on small or already-mostly-sorted subarrays, combining it with merge-sort-like merging for the overall larger structure.

theory_mcq.question: Why does heap sort achieve O(1) auxiliary space while still guaranteeing O(n log n) in ALL cases (best, average, AND worst), unlike quicksort's O(n²) worst case?
options: Heap sort doesn't actually guarantee O(n log n) in all cases; this is incorrect

Heap sort builds and maintains its sorting structure (a heap) IN-PLACE within the original array (requiring no auxiliary array like merge sort, and no recursive partitioning that depends on pivot luck like quicksort) — its heap-based extraction process guarantees O(log n) work per extraction REGARDLESS of the input's initial arrangement, since heap operations don't depend on a 'lucky' or 'unlucky' choice the way quicksort's pivot selection does
Heap sort is identical to quicksort with a different name
Heap sort only works correctly on arrays of size less than 100
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact table entry: Heap Sort has IDENTICAL worst/average/best time complexity (all O(n log n)) and O(1) space — this guaranteed consistency (no input-dependent worst case like quicksort) combined with no auxiliary array requirement (unlike merge sort) is exactly why the lesson notes it's preferred 'when O(1) space and guaranteed O(n log n) required', despite its noted trade-off of 'Poor cache perf.'

logic_mcq.question: Per the lesson's comparison table, which sorting algorithms are marked as STABLE, and what do Merge Sort, Insertion Sort, Counting Sort, and TimSort have in common that, say, Quick Sort and Heap Sort lack?
options: All algorithms in the table are equally stable

Merge Sort, Insertion Sort, Counting Sort, Bubble Sort, and TimSort are marked stable (true), while Selection Sort, Quick Sort, and Heap Sort are marked unstable (false) — the common thread among the stable algorithms is that their core mechanics (merging with <=, shifting one element at a time, frequency-based placement) naturally preserve the relative order of equal elements, while the unstable algorithms' mechanics (swapping distant elements via selection or partitioning, or heap reordering) can disrupt original relative ordering
Stability only applies to algorithms with O(n log n) complexity
Quick Sort is actually marked stable in the lesson's table
logic_mcq.explanation: Reading directly from the lesson's table: Bubble Sort (stable:true), Selection Sort (stable:false), Insertion Sort (stable:true), Merge Sort (stable:true), Quick Sort (stable:false), Heap Sort (stable:false), Counting Sort (stable:true), TimSort (stable:true) — the stable algorithms share mechanics that don't require swapping non-adjacent equal elements past each other, while the unstable ones (involving partitioning or heap restructuring) can disrupt original ordering among equal elements.

logic_mcq.question: Per the lesson's interview decision guide, if asked to 'sort objects by a field while preserving the original order of objects with equal field values', which algorithms would be APPROPRIATE choices, and why?
options: Quick Sort, since it's generally the fastest algorithm

Merge Sort or TimSort — both are explicitly marked STABLE in the comparison table, meaning they guarantee equal-field objects retain their original relative order, which directly satisfies the 'preserving order' requirement; an unstable algorithm like Quick Sort or Heap Sort could silently reorder equal elements, violating this requirement even while still producing a 'correctly sorted by field' result
Selection Sort, since it minimizes the number of swaps
Any sorting algorithm would work equally well for this requirement
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit decision guide entry: "'Sort objects by field, preserve order' -> stable sort needed -> merge or TimSort" — the stability requirement specifically rules out unstable algorithms (Quick Sort, Heap Sort, Selection Sort), even though those algorithms would still correctly sort by the field value; only stable algorithms additionally guarantee the preservation of original relative order among ties.

syntax_mcq.question: In the `sortingAlgorithms` array of objects, each entry has a `useCase` STRING field. What kind of information does this field convey, as distinguished from the `timeWorst`/`timeAvg`/`timeBest` fields?

lessons.title: Binary Search On Sorted Arrays
lessons.objective: Implement binary search with correct loop invariants, solve all four canonical binary search variants, and recognise the O(log n) search signal in any problem.
concepts: Binary search precondition: sorted array
Loop invariant: target is always in [lo, hi]
Termination: lo > hi means target absent
Mid calculation: lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2) to avoid overflow
Three-way branch: equal, less, greater
Variant 1: find exact value
Variant 2: find leftmost occurrence (lower bound)
Variant 3: find rightmost occurrence (upper bound)
Variant 4: find insertion position
lessons.explanation: Binary search finds a target in a sorted array in O(log n) by halving the search space on every step. The invariant: at every iteration, if the target exists in the array, it is somewhere in the range [lo, hi]. The algorithm maintains this invariant: compute mid = lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2), compare arr[mid] to target. If equal, found. If target is less, it must be in [lo, mid-1], so set hi = mid-1. If target is greater, it must be in [mid+1, hi], so set lo = mid+1. Termination: when lo > hi, the range is empty and the target is absent. The mid calculation uses lo + (hi - lo) / 2 instead of (lo + hi) / 2 to prevent integer overflow when lo and hi are large (irrelevant in JavaScript since numbers are floats, but critical in Java/C++ and good habit). The leftmost variant (find first occurrence of target): when arr[mid] === target, record mid as a candidate answer but continue searching left by setting hi = mid - 1. This finds the leftmost occurrence. The rightmost variant mirrors this by setting lo = mid + 1 when equal.
lessons.analogy: Binary search is how you find a name in a phone book. Open to the middle. If your name comes before the middle name, tear off the right half and open the middle of the left half. Repeat. Each step eliminates half the remaining pages. 1000 pages: 10 steps. 1,000,000 pages: 20 steps. Searching page by page (linear search) would take up to 1,000,000 steps. This is the O(log n) to O(n) difference made tangible.

code_example.explanation: Variant 4 uses lo < hi (not lo <= hi) and hi = arr.length (not arr.length-1). These are the correct invariant for finding a lower bound: lo converges to the first position where arr[i] >= target. The loop exits when lo === hi, and lo is the answer. Getting these boundary conditions wrong is the source of off-by-one bugs in binary search — always trace through a small example to verify before submitting.

common_mistakes: Using (lo + hi) / 2 for mid instead of lo + (hi - lo) / 2 — in languages with fixed-size integers (Java, C++), this causes integer overflow when lo and hi are both near INT_MAX; develop the correct habit even in JavaScript
Using lo < hi instead of lo <= hi for the exact-match variant — lo < hi exits one step early and can miss the case where lo === hi and arr[lo] is the target; use lo <= hi for exact match

Not handling the 'insertion position' variant correctly by setting hi = arr.length (not arr.length - 1) — if the target is larger than all elements, the insertion position is arr.length; an hi of arr.length - 1 would return the wrong position
lessons.interview_relevance: Binary search is Blind 75 (#704 Binary Search, #33 Search in Rotated Sorted Array, #153 Find Minimum in Rotated Array, #74 Search a 2D Matrix). The leftmost/rightmost variants are tested in #34 Find First and Last Position. Off-by-one bugs in binary search are the most common reason candidates fail otherwise-correct solutions. Tracing through a three-element array on paper before coding eliminates 90% of these bugs.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement all four variants above, then solve these three: (1) Given a sorted array with duplicates [1,2,2,2,3,4], count how many times 2 appears using only binary search (no linear scan). Use upperBound - lowerBound + 1. (2) Implement sqrt(x) using binary search: find the integer square root of x (floor(sqrt(x))) without using Math.sqrt. Binary search on the range [0, x]. (3) Given a sorted 2D matrix where each row is sorted and the first element of each row is greater than the last element of the previous row, search for a target in O(log(m*n)).

visual_explanation.description: Draw four separate binary search traces on [1,2,2,2,3,4] searching for 2. Each trace shows lo, hi, mid at each step and which direction they move. Variant 1 (exact): finds first 2 at index 1 or 2 — any valid index. Variant 2 (leftmost): always goes left when found — converges to index 1. Variant 3 (rightmost): always goes right when found — converges to index 3. Variant 4 (insert position): shows insert position for target=2.5 → index 4. Annotate the KEY DIFFERENCE: leftmost sets hi=mid-1 on match; rightmost sets lo=mid+1 on match. These are mirror images.

interview_war_story.story: The problem was Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array (#34). The candidate said 'binary search twice — once for lower bound, once for upper bound.' Correct. They coded lowerBound perfectly. For upperBound they wrote 'when arr[mid]===target, hi=mid-1.' Wrong — that searches LEFT, same as lowerBound. The interviewer asked: 'What should differ between lowerBound and upperBound?' The candidate traced through [1,2,2,2,3] looking for 2. 'In lowerBound I go left when I find a match (hi=mid-1). In upperBound I go RIGHT (lo=mid+1).' Fixed in 30 seconds. The distinction: when target found, lowerBound searches left, upperBound searches right.
interview_war_story.lesson: Lower bound: when equal, go left (hi=mid-1, record candidate). Upper bound: when equal, go right (lo=mid+1, record candidate). The only difference is one line.

questions.question: Why use lo + Math.floor((hi-lo)/2) instead of Math.floor((lo+hi)/2) for computing mid?
options: The first is faster
In languages with fixed-size integers (Java, C++), (lo+hi) can overflow if both are near INT_MAX. lo+(hi-lo)/2 avoids this. Good practice even in JavaScript where numbers are 64-bit floats.
Both are always correct
The second is more readable and preferred
questions.explanation: (lo+hi) can overflow in languages with fixed-size integers when lo+hi > INT_MAX. lo+(hi-lo)/2 avoids this because (hi-lo) is always small (a difference, not a sum). JavaScript uses 64-bit floats (max safe integer ~9×10^15) so overflow is unlikely in practice, but the habit is important for Java/C++ interviews where this is a common bug.

questions.question: Binary search for exact match uses 'while (lo <= hi)'. Binary search for insertion position uses 'while (lo < hi)'. Why the difference?
options: They are interchangeable — use either

Exact match: lo=hi is still a valid check (that single element might be the target). Insertion position: lo=hi means the range has converged to one slot — that IS the answer, so we exit. The different conditions reflect different invariants.
while(lo<hi) is always correct
while(lo<=hi) causes infinite loops
questions.explanation: Exact match (lo<=hi): when lo=hi, arr[lo] might be the target — must check it. Insertion position (lo<hi): uses hi=mid (not mid-1) when arr[mid]>=target, so hi can equal lo — the loop must stop. Using lo<=hi with hi=mid would loop forever when lo=hi. Different invariants require different termination conditions.

questions.question: Count the occurrences of value 2 in [1,2,2,2,3,4] using only binary search. What approach?
options: Linear scan — binary search cannot count occurrences
Find rightmost occurrence (upper bound) and leftmost occurrence (lower bound). Count = upperBound - lowerBound + 1
Divide array in half and count in each half
Sort first, then scan
questions.explanation: lowerBound([1,2,2,2,3,4], 2) = 1 (first index of 2). upperBound([1,2,2,2,3,4], 2) = 3 (last index of 2). Count = 3 - 1 + 1 = 3. This is O(log n) — two binary searches. No linear scan needed.

Then solve: given [1,2,2,2,3,4], count occurrences of 2 using only binary search. Also solve: integer square root of x (floor(sqrt(x))) using binary search on [0,x].

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: Using lo < hi for exact match can miss the answer when lo=hi. The single element at lo=hi might be the target but the loop exits before checking it.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(log n) but misses single-element case

hints.text: upperBound: when arr[mid]===target, record result=mid then set lo=mid+1 (search right). mySqrt: binary search on [1,x]. When mid*mid<=x: record result=mid and set lo=mid+1. When mid*mid>x: set hi=mid-1. Return result.

mySqrt: maintain invariant that result is the largest k found so far where k*k<=x. When mid*mid<x, mid is a candidate — update result and search higher. When mid*mid>x, search lower. Return result after loop.
upperBound when equal: result=mid;lo=mid+1. mySqrt: if(mid*mid<=x){result=mid;lo=mid+1;}else hi=mid-1; return result after loop.

theory_mcq.question: What is the critical PRECONDITION for binary search to work correctly, and what happens if this precondition is violated?
options: Binary search requires the array to contain only positive numbers

Binary search REQUIRES the input array to be SORTED — the entire algorithm relies on being able to eliminate half the remaining search space based on a single comparison (if arr[mid] is too small/large, an entire half can be safely discarded), which is only valid if elements are in sorted order; on an UNSORTED array, this elimination logic breaks down and the algorithm can produce incorrect results (potentially missing the target even though it exists in the array)
Binary search works equally well on sorted and unsorted arrays
The precondition only matters for arrays larger than 1000 elements
theory_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's explicit statement: 'Binary search precondition: sorted array' — the algorithm's core logic (comparing the target to the middle element to decide which half to discard) is only mathematically valid when the array's sortedness guarantees that 'too small' or 'too large' correctly implies the target can't be in the corresponding half.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson use `lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2)` to compute the midpoint, rather than the more commonly seen `Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2)`?
options: Both formulas are mathematically equivalent in EVERY case, with no practical difference

While mathematically equivalent for reasonable values, `lo + (hi-lo)/2` is described as 'overflow-safe' — in languages with FIXED-size integer types, `lo + hi` could exceed the maximum representable integer value when both lo and hi are very large, causing integer overflow and producing an incorrect midpoint; computing the OFFSET from lo first (hi-lo, which is always smaller than hi alone) and adding it back avoids ever summing two large numbers together
The two formulas produce systematically different (and both equally valid) results
This formula is required specifically for JavaScript and wouldn't work in other languages
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit code comment: 'lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2) to avoid overflow' — this is a well-known defensive coding pattern from languages with fixed-width integers (like Java's 32-bit int), where lo+hi could overflow if both are near the maximum representable value; JavaScript's numbers don't have this exact overflow issue at typical array sizes, but the lesson teaches the universally-safe pattern as good practice.

logic_mcq.question: What is the key behavioral difference between `lowerBound` (Variant 2) and `upperBound` (Variant 3) when the target appears MULTIPLE times in the array?
options: There is no difference; both return the same index

When a match is found (`arr[mid] === target`), lowerBound records it as a candidate and continues searching LEFT (`hi = mid - 1`, looking for an even earlier occurrence), while upperBound records it as a candidate and continues searching RIGHT (`lo = mid + 1`, looking for an even later occurrence) — this opposite continuation direction is what makes lowerBound converge on the FIRST (leftmost) occurrence and upperBound converge on the LAST (rightmost) occurrence
lowerBound only works on arrays with no duplicates
upperBound always returns -1 when duplicates exist
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the precise mechanism distinguishing the two variants: both find A match and then deliberately CONTINUE searching in the relevant direction (rather than stopping immediately) to find the boundary — lowerBound shrinks `hi` to search further left for an earlier occurrence, upperBound grows `lo` to search further right for a later occurrence, with the LAST recorded `result` before the loop terminates being the true boundary.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `searchInsertPosition([1,3,5,6], target=2)` per the lesson's own stated result. Why does this function return 1, even though 2 doesn't EXIST in the array at all?
options: This is an error; the function should return -1 for values not present

searchInsertPosition (Variant 4) isn't searching for an EXISTING match — it's finding the correct index where the target COULD BE INSERTED to keep the array sorted; since 2 would need to be inserted between 1 (index 0) and 3 (index 1) to maintain sorted order, the correct insertion position is index 1, which is exactly what the function (and the lesson's stated result) confirms
The function returns 1 because that's always the default return value
searchInsertPosition only works for values that already exist in the array
logic_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's exact stated result: '[1,3,5,6], target=5 -> 2. target=2 -> 1. target=7 -> 4' — Variant 4 is fundamentally different from the other three: it doesn't require the target to EXIST in the array, instead finding where it WOULD belong to preserve sorted order, confirmed by direct execution to correctly return 1 for target=2.

logic_mcq.question: Why does `searchInsertPosition` use a half-open range convention (`hi = arr.length`, looping while `lo < hi`) instead of the closed-range convention (`hi = arr.length - 1`, looping while `lo <= hi`) used in the other three variants?
options: This is an inconsistency/bug; all four variants should use the identical convention

Since the target may need to be inserted AT THE VERY END of the array (a position that doesn't correspond to any EXISTING valid index, but rather to the position 'one past the last element'), the half-open convention (hi starting at arr.length, representing an exclusive upper bound) naturally accommodates this 'insert at the end' case without needing special-case logic — when the loop terminates (lo===hi), lo directly gives the correct insertion position, including the edge case where it equals arr.length itself
The half-open convention makes the algorithm run faster
JavaScript requires different loop conventions depending on array size
logic_mcq.explanation: This is a deliberate design choice reflecting the different SEMANTIC purpose of Variant 4: since 'insert at the end' is a valid answer (target larger than every element), the search space needs to naturally include the position AFTER the last index — the half-open convention (hi=length, lo<hi loop condition) is the standard way to express 'a range of valid insertion points including one-past-the-end', confirmed by the lesson's own example showing target=7 correctly returning 4 (one past the last valid index 3) for a 4-element array.

syntax_mcq.question: In `else hi = mid;` within `searchInsertPosition`, why does this branch set `hi = mid` (KEEPING mid as a still-possible answer) rather than `hi = mid - 1` (as the other binary search variants do when narrowing)?
options: This is a bug; it should be hi = mid - 1 for consistency

This branch executes when `arr[mid] >= target`, meaning mid COULD be the correct insertion position (or the answer might be even earlier) — since mid itself remains a VALID CANDIDATE answer (not definitively ruled out the way it would be in an exact-match search), excluding it from the search range (via mid-1) would incorrectly discard a potentially correct answer; keeping hi=mid preserves mid as still-reachable while continuing to search for an even better (earlier) candidate
hi = mid always evaluates to the same value as hi = mid - 1
This syntax only works correctly when the array has an even number of elements
syntax_mcq.explanation: This reflects the half-open range's semantics: when arr[mid] >= target, mid is a VALID candidate for the insertion position (everything from mid onward is >= target) — narrowing to hi=mid (rather than mid-1) correctly keeps mid INCLUDED in the remaining search range [lo, hi), since it might still be the precise answer or an earlier index might be even better.

lessons.title: Search In Rotated Sorted Array
lessons.objective: Apply binary search to a rotated sorted array by using a two-condition check to determine which half is sorted at every step.
concepts: Rotated sorted array: sorted array shifted at a pivot point
Key insight: one half is always fully sorted
Determine sorted half: compare arr[lo] with arr[mid]
Check if target is in the sorted half
Recurse on the half containing the target
With duplicates: cannot determine sorted half when arr[lo] === arr[mid]
Duplicates variant: shrink lo by 1 when equal
O(log n) without duplicates, O(n) worst case with duplicates
lessons.explanation: A rotated sorted array like [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] is a sorted array that has been shifted. Standard binary search fails because the array is not globally sorted. The key insight that enables O(log n) anyway: after computing mid, one of the two halves [lo..mid] or [mid+1..hi] is always fully sorted. You can determine which one by comparing arr[lo] with arr[mid]. If arr[lo] <= arr[mid], the left half [lo..mid] is fully sorted. Otherwise, the right half [mid+1..hi] is fully sorted. Once you know which half is sorted, check whether the target falls within that sorted half's range. If yes, recurse into that half. If no, recurse into the other half. This maintains O(log n) by eliminating half the search space on each step. With duplicates (arr[lo] === arr[mid]), you cannot determine which half is sorted. The safe approach: shrink lo by 1 (or hi by 1) and continue. In the worst case (all duplicates except one), this degrades to O(n).
lessons.analogy: Searching a rotated array is like finding your name in a phone book where someone accidentally shuffled the middle section. Open to the middle. Check if the left half has consecutive letters (fully sorted). If yes, your name is either in that sorted left half or somewhere in the jumbled right. Check the first and last letter of the sorted half to decide. One half is always tidy, one may be jumbled. You eliminate the half that definitely cannot contain your name.

code_example.explanation: The condition nums[lo] <= nums[mid] (not <) is critical. When lo === mid (two-element subarray), nums[lo] === nums[mid] and the left half is trivially sorted (one element). Using <= correctly handles this case. The check target < nums[mid] (strict) is also important: if target equals nums[mid] we already returned, so we only reach this point when target != nums[mid].

common_mistakes: Using nums[lo] < nums[mid] instead of <= to detect the sorted half — when lo === mid (two elements remain), nums[lo] === nums[mid] and the left half is sorted; <= correctly identifies this
Not accounting for the case where target equals nums[mid] at the start of the loop body — always check nums[mid] === target first before determining which half to search

Applying the no-duplicates algorithm to an array with duplicates and getting wrong answers — duplicates must be handled with the lo++/hi-- shrink; always confirm with the interviewer whether duplicates are possible
lessons.interview_relevance: Search in Rotated Sorted Array (#33) is Blind 75. Search in Rotated Sorted Array II (with duplicates, #81) is NeetCode 150. Both appear frequently at mid-level interviews. The key insight — 'one half is always sorted, use that half's bounds to decide where to recurse' — must be articulable in one sentence before coding.

Then solve the search problem by: (1) finding the pivot, (2) determining which half is fully sorted (no rotation), and (3) running standard binary search on the correct half. Compare this two-step approach with the single-pass approach above and state which is cleaner and why.

visual_explanation.description: Trace [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] searching for target=0. Step 1: lo=0,hi=6,mid=3. nums[3]=7. nums[0]=4<=nums[3]=7: LEFT sorted=[4,5,6,7]. Is 4<=0<7? No. Search right: lo=4. Step 2: lo=4,hi=6,mid=5. nums[5]=1. nums[4]=0<=nums[5]=1: LEFT sorted=[0,1]. Is 0<=0<1? Yes. Search left: hi=4. Step 3: lo=4,hi=4,mid=4. nums[4]=0===target. Return 4. Draw each step as a highlighted array with lo,mid,hi pointers and shaded sorted half. Label: 'At each step: identify sorted half, check if target is in it, recurse into the half that contains target'.

interview_war_story.story: The problem was Search in Rotated Sorted Array. The candidate said: 'One half is always sorted. Compare arr[lo] and arr[mid] to find which.' Correct start. They coded it but used strict < in 'nums[lo] < nums[mid]'. The interviewer said: 'What happens when lo=4 and hi=5?' Candidate traced: lo=4, hi=5, mid=4. nums[lo]=nums[mid]. Strict < is false — code thinks right half is sorted. But left half [lo..mid] is a single element — trivially sorted. Wrong branch selected. The candidate changed < to <=. 'Why does <= matter?' Candidate: 'When lo=mid, the left half is one element — trivially sorted. <= correctly identifies it as the sorted half.'
interview_war_story.lesson: Use nums[lo] <= nums[mid] (with <=) to identify the sorted half. The = handles the two-element subarray case where lo=mid and the single-element left half is trivially sorted.

questions.question: In a rotated sorted array, after computing mid, how do you determine which half is sorted?
options: Check if arr[mid] is less than arr[hi]
Check if arr[lo] <= arr[mid] — if true, left half [lo..mid] is fully sorted; otherwise right half [mid+1..hi] is sorted
Check if arr[mid] > arr[lo]
You cannot determine which half is sorted without checking all elements
questions.explanation: If arr[lo] <= arr[mid]: the left half [lo..mid] is monotonically increasing (fully sorted). The rotation point, if any, is in the right half. If arr[lo] > arr[mid]: the right half [mid+1..hi] is fully sorted. The rotation point is in the left half. Note: <= not < because when lo=mid (two elements), arr[lo]=arr[mid] and the left is trivially sorted.

questions.question: For target=0 in [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]: after identifying left half [4,5,6,7] as sorted, how do you decide which half to recurse into?
options: Always recurse into the sorted half
Check if target is in the sorted half's range [4..7]. Target=0 is NOT in [4..7], so recurse into the OTHER half (right side [0,1,2]).
Recurse into both halves
Check arr[mid] first
questions.explanation: Once the sorted half is identified, check if the target falls within that sorted half's range. For target=0 and sorted left [4,5,6,7]: 4<=0 is false, so 0 is NOT in [4..7]. Recurse into the unsorted right half. This eliminates half the search space, maintaining O(log n).

questions.question: Why does adding duplicates to a rotated array degrade binary search from O(log n) to O(n) worst case?
options: Duplicates prevent sorting

When arr[lo]===arr[mid], you cannot determine which half is sorted — both halves start with the same value. The safe fix is to shrink lo++ (or hi--) by 1, making only O(1) progress instead of O(n/2). In the worst case [1,1,1,0,1,1,1], you must shrink n times.
Duplicates cause the array not to be sorted
Duplicates make binary search impossible
questions.explanation: With arr[lo]===arr[mid]: you cannot distinguish [1,1,...,0,...,1] (rotation in left half) from [1,1,...,1,...,1] (no rotation). The only safe action is to shrink lo++ — O(1) progress. In the worst case with all duplicates except one, this takes O(n) total steps.

theory_mcq.question: What is the single key insight that makes binary search applicable to a ROTATED sorted array, even though the array as a whole is no longer fully sorted?
options: Rotated arrays are actually still fully sorted; rotation doesn't change anything

Even though the WHOLE array isn't sorted, AT LEAST ONE of the two halves (split at any midpoint) is ALWAYS fully sorted — by comparing `arr[lo]` to `arr[mid]`, you can determine WHICH half is the sorted one, and then check whether the target falls within that sorted half's value range to decide which half to recurse into, preserving the O(log n) elimination strategy despite the rotation
Binary search cannot actually be applied to rotated arrays; the lesson's premise is false
Rotation only affects the first element, so binary search works unchanged on the rest
theory_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's explicit key insight: 'Key insight: one half is always fully sorted' — a single rotation point means that splitting the array anywhere always leaves at least one contiguous half that's internally sorted (since the rotation 'break' can only occur in one of the two halves), and this property is what makes binary search's halving logic still applicable.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the presence of DUPLICATE values in a rotated sorted array degrade the search from O(log n) to O(n) worst case?
options: Duplicates have no actual effect on the algorithm's complexity

When `nums[lo] === nums[mid]` (which can ONLY happen with duplicate values, since a strictly sorted-then-rotated array would never have equal endpoints of a sub-range unless duplicates exist), the algorithm CANNOT determine which half is the sorted one (the comparison that normally reveals this becomes uninformative) — the lesson's duplicate-handling fallback resorts to shrinking the search range by just ONE element at a time (`lo++; hi--;`) in this ambiguous case, which can degrade to linear O(n) behavior in the worst case (e.g., an array of all identical values except one rotation point)
Duplicates always cause the algorithm to enter an infinite loop
Duplicates only matter if there are more than 1000 of them
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact explanation: 'With duplicates: cannot determine sorted half when arr[lo] === arr[mid]' and 'O(1) progress, O(n) worst case total' — without duplicates, comparing arr[lo] to arr[mid] always reliably reveals which half is sorted; duplicates can make this comparison ambiguous (both sides could appear 'equal' even when only one is truly sorted), forcing a fallback to a much slower one-element-at-a-time elimination strategy.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `searchRotated([4,5,6,7,0,1,2], target=0)` per the lesson's own worked example. At the FIRST iteration (lo=0, hi=6, mid=3), which half is determined to be sorted, and what decision is made?
options: The right half is determined sorted, and the search continues there

Since nums[lo]=4 <= nums[mid]=7, the LEFT half [4,5,6,7] is determined to be sorted; checking if target (0) falls within this sorted range (4<=0? No), the target is determined to NOT be in the left half, so the search moves to the right half by setting lo=4 — confirmed by direct execution
The algorithm immediately returns -1 at this step
Both halves are determined to be unsorted, requiring a different algorithm
logic_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's exact trace, independently re-verified by direct execution producing the correct final answer of index 4: 'nums[0]=4 <= nums[3]=7: left [4,5,6,7] is sorted... 4<=0? No -> target not in left half -> lo=4' — since 0 doesn't fall within the sorted left half's range [4,7], the algorithm correctly concludes the target must be in the other half.

logic_mcq.question: Continuing the same trace, at the second iteration (lo=4, hi=6, mid=5), why does the algorithm conclude the target IS in the sorted left portion this time, leading to hi=4 and eventually finding the answer?
options: This is inconsistent with the first iteration's logic

At this point, nums[lo]=0 <= nums[mid]=1, so the LEFT portion [0,1] (within this sub-range) is determined to be sorted; checking if target (0) falls within this range (0<=0 && 0<1? Yes), the target IS determined to be in this sorted left portion, so hi is narrowed to mid (hi=4), and the very next iteration finds nums[4]=0 matching the target exactly, returning index 4
The algorithm gives up and returns -1 at this point
The algorithm restarts the search from the very beginning
logic_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's exact trace: 'nums[4]=0 <= nums[5]=1: left [0,1] is sorted. 0<=0 && 0<1? Yes -> target in left half -> hi=4... lo=4 hi=4 mid=4 nums[4]=0 === target -> return 4' — the same sorted-half-determination logic is reapplied at each iteration on the CURRENT remaining sub-range, correctly narrowing down to the exact target position.

syntax_mcq.question: In `if (nums[lo] <= nums[mid])`, why is `<=` used rather than strict `<`?
options: There's no meaningful difference; either comparison operator would work identically

Using `<=` correctly handles the edge case where `lo === mid` (a sub-range containing only one or two elements, where nums[lo] and nums[mid] could be the SAME element or equal in value) — this ensures the 'left half is sorted' determination remains correct even for these small/degenerate sub-ranges, where a single element trivially counts as 'sorted'
Using <= would cause an infinite loop, and this is actually a bug
<= is required syntax in all JavaScript comparisons
syntax_mcq.explanation: The `<=` (rather than strict `<`) correctly handles boundary cases where the sub-range being examined is very small (potentially just one or two elements, where lo and mid could coincide or have equal values) — a single-element range is trivially 'sorted', and using <= ensures this edge case is correctly classified rather than accidentally treated as the 'right half is sorted' branch.

lessons.title: Find Minimum In Rotated Array
lessons.objective: Find the minimum element in a rotated sorted array in O(log n) by using the rotation break as the binary search condition.
concepts: Rotation pivot: the point where the sequence drops
Minimum element is always at the rotation pivot
Sorted half identification: compare arr[mid] with arr[hi]
If arr[mid] > arr[hi]: minimum is in right half
If arr[mid] <= arr[hi]: minimum is in left half (including mid)
Termination: lo === hi means the single remaining element is the minimum
With duplicates: O(n) worst case when arr[mid] === arr[hi]
Connection to Search In Rotated Array: finding pivot enables two-step search
lessons.explanation: In a rotated sorted array, the minimum element is at the rotation pivot — the point where the sorted sequence breaks. For [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], the minimum is 0 at index 4. The binary search approach uses a different comparison than the search problem: compare arr[mid] with arr[hi] (not arr[lo]). If arr[mid] > arr[hi], the minimum must be in the right half [mid+1..hi] because the sequence drops somewhere to the right of mid. If arr[mid] <= arr[hi], the right half is already sorted and the minimum is in the left half [lo..mid] (mid could be the minimum itself, so we include it). Note: we compare with arr[hi], not arr[lo], because the left endpoint lo is always in the 'high' portion of the rotated array. The loop terminates when lo === hi — a single element, which is the minimum.
lessons.analogy: Finding the minimum in a rotated sorted array is like finding the lowest point on a mountain range that has been 'rotated' so the peak is somewhere in the middle of your view. Look at the middle point and the rightmost point. If the middle is higher than the right, the lowest point is somewhere in the right half (the sequence goes down somewhere to the right). If the middle is lower than or equal to the right, the lowest point is in the left half or at the middle itself.

code_example.explanation: The critical distinction from Lesson 8: here we compare arr[mid] with arr[hi], while in Lesson 8 we compared arr[lo] with arr[mid]. These are different problems requiring different comparison sides. Using arr[hi] here is correct because hi is always in the 'lower' portion of the rotated array (or equal to mid), making it the stable reference point. Mixing up which side to compare is the most common bug when students try to adapt one solution to the other.

common_mistakes: Using lo < hi with hi = mid (not mid - 1) when arr[mid] <= arr[hi] — hi = mid-1 would exclude mid from the search range, potentially missing the minimum if mid is the answer; hi = mid keeps mid as a candidate
Comparing arr[mid] with arr[lo] instead of arr[hi] — this is the comparison for the Search in Rotated Array problem, not Find Minimum; they use different reference points
Returning nums[mid] instead of nums[lo] after the loop — the loop exits when lo === hi, and nums[lo] is the minimum; mid is not defined after the loop exits
lessons.interview_relevance: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array (#153) is Blind 75. Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II (with duplicates, #154) is NeetCode 150. Both are consistently asked at every major company. The two problems (#33 Search, #153 Find Minimum) together test whether you understand the rotated array structure from two different angles — searching for a target vs finding the pivot.

State the time complexity of both approaches (both are O(log n), but the two-step approach makes three binary searches total — is it still O(log n)?). visual_explanation.description: Trace [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] with find minimum algorithm. Step 1: lo=0,hi=6,mid=3. nums[3]=7, nums[6]=2. 7>2: lo=4. Step 2: lo=4,hi=6,mid=5. nums[5]=1, nums[6]=2. 1<=2: hi=5. Step 3: lo=4,hi=5,mid=4. nums[4]=0, nums[5]=1. 0<=1: hi=4. Step 4: lo=4,hi=4. Loop exits. return nums[4]=0. Draw each step as the array with a sliding search window [lo..hi] that narrows. Shade the dropped portion grey at each step. Label: 'Compare arr[mid] with arr[hi] — if mid>hi: min is RIGHT. If mid<=hi: min is LEFT OR AT MID'. Also trace [3,1,2] for contrast.

interview_war_story.story: The problem was Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array. The candidate wrote the solution but used hi=mid-1 when nums[mid]<=nums[hi]. The interviewer said: 'Test this on [2,1].' Candidate traced: lo=0,hi=1,mid=0. nums[0]=2>nums[1]=1: lo=mid+1=1. Loop exits. return nums[1]=1. Correct. Interviewer: 'Now test [1,2].' lo=0,hi=1,mid=0. nums[0]=1<=nums[1]=2: hi=mid-1=-1. Loop exits (lo=0>hi=-1). return nums[0]=1. Correct by luck. Interviewer: 'What would happen if the minimum were exactly at the mid position in a longer array?' The candidate realised: 'hi=mid-1 would skip it. I need hi=mid to keep mid as a candidate.' That insight — hi=mid not hi=mid-1 — was the entire interview.
interview_war_story.lesson: When the condition sets hi=mid (not mid-1), it is because mid is a CANDIDATE for the answer. hi=mid-1 would eliminate it. The invariant is: 'the minimum is somewhere in [lo..hi].' Narrowing with hi=mid maintains this invariant. hi=mid-1 breaks it.

questions.question: In findMin, when arr[mid] > arr[hi], where is the minimum?
options: In the left half [lo..mid]
In the right half [mid+1..hi] — arr[mid] is in the 'high' portion of the rotation, the drop to the minimum happens to its right
At arr[mid]
Cannot determine
questions.explanation: If arr[mid] > arr[hi]: arr[mid] is still in the 'before rotation' section (high values). The minimum is somewhere to the right — in [mid+1..hi]. So lo=mid+1. If arr[mid] <= arr[hi]: arr[mid] could be the minimum itself or the minimum is in [lo..mid]. So hi=mid (keep mid as a candidate).

questions.question: findMin uses 'while (lo < hi)' and 'hi = mid' (not mid-1) when arr[mid]<=arr[hi]. Why 'hi=mid' and not 'hi=mid-1'?
options: Typo — should be mid-1
hi=mid keeps mid as a candidate for the minimum. If we used hi=mid-1, we might eliminate the actual minimum (arr[mid] could be the minimum itself). lo<hi exits when they converge at the answer.
Both are equivalent
Performance optimisation
questions.explanation: When arr[mid]<=arr[hi], arr[mid] could be the minimum. Using hi=mid-1 would exclude mid from the search range and potentially miss the minimum. hi=mid narrows the range while keeping mid as a candidate. The loop exits when lo=hi — the single remaining element is the minimum.

questions.question: findMin compares arr[mid] with arr[hi]. findRotatedSearch compares arr[lo] with arr[mid]. Why do these two problems use different comparison sides?
options: They are the same — the comparison side does not matter

findMin uses arr[hi] as the reference because hi is always in the 'low' part of the rotated array (or equal to mid) — arr[hi] is the stable lower reference. findRotatedSearch uses arr[lo] to determine which half is sorted from the left side.
Random choice
Implementation preference
questions.explanation: findMin: we compare arr[mid] with arr[hi] because arr[hi] is always in the lower section of the rotated array, making it a stable reference for 'is arr[mid] in the high section?'. Search in rotated: we compare arr[lo] with arr[mid] to determine whether the LEFT half is sorted. These are different questions requiring different reference points.

But on [1,2]: lo=0,hi=1,mid=0: nums[0]=1<=nums[1]=2 so hi=mid-1=-1. lo=0>hi=-1: loop exits. Returns nums[0]=1. Correct BUT the invariant is broken — it worked by luck. hi=mid is the safe invariant.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(log n) but may return wrong answer when mid is the minimum

optimal_solution.complexity: findMin: O(log n). findMinWithDuplicates: O(log n) average, O(n) worst. searchViaPivot: O(log n) — three binary searches total, still O(log n).

hints.text: findMin loop condition: while(lo<hi) — exits when lo=hi. Inside: if(nums[mid]>nums[hi]) lo=mid+1 (min is right of mid). Else hi=mid (min is at mid or left of mid — keep mid as candidate). After loop: return nums[lo].

Why hi=mid and not hi=mid-1: when nums[mid]<=nums[hi], mid could be the minimum. Using hi=mid-1 would exclude it. Using hi=mid keeps it as a candidate while still narrowing the range. The loop exits at lo=hi — the single remaining candidate.

theory_mcq.question: Why is the minimum element of a rotated sorted array always located precisely at the 'rotation pivot' (the point where the sequence drops)?
options: The minimum could be anywhere in the array with equal probability

Before rotation, the array was sorted in ASCENDING order, meaning the smallest element was originally at index 0; rotation shifts elements circularly, but the RELATIVE ascending order within each contiguous segment is preserved — the only place where a 'larger value immediately followed by a smaller value' (a drop) occurs is exactly at the rotation point, which must be where the smallest overall element sits, since everything before the drop is larger than everything after it (up to the drop) within the original ascending sequence
The minimum is always at index 0 regardless of rotation
The minimum's position is undefined and cannot be determined algorithmically
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit insight: 'Minimum element is always at the rotation pivot' — since the array was originally sorted ascending before rotation, the only 'break' in ascending order occurs at the rotation point, and the element immediately after that break is necessarily the smallest value in the entire array (since it was originally at index 0 of the unrotated sequence).

theory_mcq.question: Why does `findMin` compare `nums[mid]` against `nums[hi]` (rather than against `nums[lo]`, as `searchRotated` does) to decide which half to search?
options: This is an arbitrary choice with no functional difference from comparing against nums[lo]

Comparing mid against HI specifically allows the algorithm to determine whether the MINIMUM lies in the right half (if nums[mid] > nums[hi], the drop/rotation point must be somewhere to the right of mid, since values increasing past mid but exceeding the rightmost value signals an unresolved drop ahead) or in the left half INCLUDING mid itself (if nums[mid] <= nums[hi], everything from mid to hi is already in proper ascending order, meaning the drop — and thus the minimum — must be at or before mid) — this specific comparison choice is what correctly narrows toward the pivot point
Comparing against nums[hi] is required because nums[lo] is always undefined
This comparison method only works for arrays with an odd number of elements
theory_mcq.explanation: The choice to compare mid against hi (rather than lo) is specifically suited to FINDING THE MINIMUM (the pivot point itself), as distinguished from searchRotated's goal of finding an arbitrary target value — comparing against hi reveals whether the right portion [mid, hi] is fully sorted (nums[mid] <= nums[hi], meaning no rotation break exists in that range, so the pivot must be at or before mid) or not (nums[mid] > nums[hi], meaning the break/minimum is somewhere after mid).

logic_mcq.question: Trace `findMin([4,5,6,7,0,1,2])` per the lesson's own worked example, confirmed by direct execution. What is the sequence of (lo, hi, mid) values, and what is the final answer?
options: (0,6,3): nums[3]=7 > nums[6]=2, so lo=4. (4,6,5): nums[5]=1 <= nums[6]=2, so hi=5. (4,5,4): nums[4]=0 <= nums[5]=1, so hi=4. Loop exits (lo===hi===4) -> return nums[4] = 0 — confirmed correct by direct execution
The function immediately returns nums[0]=4 without any iterations
The loop never terminates for this input
logic_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's exact trace, independently re-verified by direct execution: 'lo=0 hi=6 mid=3 nums[3]=7 nums[6]=2: 7>2 -> lo=4... lo=4 hi=6 mid=5... 1<=2 -> hi=5... lo=4 hi=5 mid=4... 0<=1 -> hi=4... lo=4 hi=4: loop exits -> return nums[4] = 0 correct' — three iterations correctly narrow the search to the true minimum at index 4.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `findMin([1])` per the lesson's own worked example — a SINGLE-element array with no actual rotation. Why does the function return the correct answer WITHOUT the while loop ever executing even once?
options: This is a special-cased error condition that returns a default value

The while loop's condition is `lo < hi`; for a single-element array, lo and hi are BOTH initialized to 0 (the only valid index), so `lo < hi` (0 < 0) is immediately FALSE, and the loop body never executes — the function falls straight through to `return nums[lo]`, which correctly returns nums[0] (the only element, and trivially the minimum of a one-element array)
The function throws an error for single-element arrays
The loop executes exactly once regardless of array size
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: 'TRACE on [1] (single element, no rotation): lo=0 hi=0: loop never runs -> return nums[0] = 1 correct' — this demonstrates the algorithm correctly handles the degenerate single-element edge case automatically, simply because the loop's entry condition naturally evaluates to false when lo and hi start equal.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `findMin([3,1,2])` per the lesson's own worked example. Why does the FIRST comparison (nums[mid]=1 vs nums[hi]=2) lead to narrowing via `hi=mid` rather than `lo=mid+1`?
options: This is inconsistent with the algorithm's stated logic

Since nums[mid]=1 <= nums[hi]=2 (the condition for the 'else' branch, narrowing via hi=mid), this indicates the right portion [mid, hi] is already in correctly ascending order (no rotation break within it), meaning the rotation pivot (and thus the minimum) must be located at or BEFORE mid — confirmed by direct execution producing the correct final answer of nums[1]=1
The algorithm always defaults to hi=mid regardless of the comparison result
This trace produces an incorrect result; the lesson's example is flawed
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace, independently re-verified by direct execution: 'lo=0 hi=2 mid=1 nums[1]=1 nums[2]=2: 1<=2 -> hi=1... lo=0 hi=1 mid=0 nums[0]=3 nums[1]=1: 3>1 -> lo=1... lo=1 hi=1: loop exits -> return nums[1] = 1 correct' — the algorithm correctly identifies that since the right portion is already sorted, the pivot (minimum) must be at index <= mid, narrowing the search leftward.

syntax_mcq.question: In `findMinWithDuplicates`, why does the function use a THREE-way branch (`if/else if/else`) comparing `nums[mid]` to `nums[hi]`, rather than the simpler TWO-way branch (`if/else`) used in the no-duplicates `findMin`?
options: The three-way branch is purely stylistic with no functional necessity

With duplicates allowed, `nums[mid]` could be EQUAL to `nums[hi]` (a case impossible to definitively classify as 'sorted' or 'not sorted' using only greater-than/less-than comparisons) — the three-way branch explicitly handles this AMBIGUOUS equal case separately (`hi--`, making minimal guaranteed-safe progress) from the two UNAMBIGUOUS cases (`nums[mid] > nums[hi]` meaning search right, `nums[mid] < nums[hi]` meaning search left/include mid), which is exactly the source of the O(n) worst-case degradation when duplicates are present
The three-way branch only matters for arrays with negative numbers
This is required JavaScript syntax for any array containing duplicate values
syntax_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's explicit explanation: 'nums[mid] === nums[hi]: cannot tell, shrink hi' — without duplicates, the simple two-way branch is sufficient since nums[mid] and nums[hi] can never coincidentally be equal in a way that creates ambiguity; with duplicates, this equality becomes possible and genuinely uninformative, requiring the explicit ambiguous-case fallback that degrades performance to O(n) worst case.

lessons.title: Sorting And Searching Problem Thinking
lessons.objective: Apply the sorting and binary search decision tree to any new problem, recognise the O(log n) signal, and map all Module 5 Blind 75 problems to their correct pattern.
concepts: O(log n) recognition signal: 'sorted array', 'search', 'find minimum/maximum in constraint'
Binary search on the answer: applying binary search to a value range, not an array
Sort-then-search: when sorting enables an O(n log n) solution vs O(n²) naive
Sorting as a preprocessing step for two-pointer and greedy problems
Divide and conquer beyond sorting: merge sort structure applies to many problems
Module 5 Blind 75 problems mapped to patterns
Skills unlocked: Sorting, Binary Search, Divide and Conquer
Bridge to Module 6: linked lists use the same divide-and-conquer structure
lessons.explanation: Module 5 introduces two types of pattern recognition. First: O(log n) signal. Any problem mentioning 'sorted array', 'find in sorted', 'search', or asking for a minimum or maximum under a monotonic condition is a binary search candidate. The 'binary search on the answer' technique extends this: if the answer is a number in a range [lo, hi] and you can check in O(n) whether a given candidate answer is feasible, you can binary search on the answer space in O(n log n) total. Second: sort-first strategy. Many O(n²) naive solutions become O(n log n) or O(n) after sorting, because sorting eliminates the need to compare every pair. Three Sum (Module 3) sorts first then uses two pointers. Meeting Rooms problems sort by start time then scan linearly. This sort-first pattern is one of the highest-leverage reductions in competitive programming and interviews.
lessons.analogy: Sorting is like lining up students by height before asking questions about them. Once sorted, 'is there anyone exactly 170cm?' is a binary search (O(log n)), not a scan (O(n)). 'Are there two students whose heights sum to 340cm?' becomes a two-pointer problem on a sorted array instead of a nested loop. The sorting investment (O(n log n)) pays for itself on every subsequent query.

code_example.explanation: Binary search on the answer (Koko Eating Bananas, #875) is the most important new pattern in Module 5. The template: define a check(candidate) function that returns true/false, binary search on the candidate value range. This applies to dozens of problems: minimum ship capacity, minimum days to complete tasks, split array largest sum. The check function is always O(n), giving O(n log(answer_range)) total.

common_mistakes: Not recognising binary search on the answer as a pattern — problems like 'find the minimum X such that condition Y holds' are binary search on the answer space; the condition Y must be monotonic (once it holds for X, it holds for all larger X) for binary search to apply
Sorting arrays in interview problems without a comparator and not catching the bug — always test your sort with [10,2,9] before assuming arr.sort() works correctly for numbers
Not attempting Module 5 Blind 75 problems before moving to Module 6 — binary search on rotated arrays is the hardest material in Level 1 and requires multiple practice attempts to internalise
lessons.interview_relevance: Module 5 contains five Blind 75 problems including two of the most consistently asked: Search in Rotated Sorted Array (#33) and Koko Eating Bananas (#875, binary search on answer). Completing all five from scratch with correct complexity analysis and loop invariant articulation is the measurable outcome of this module.

For each: apply the 5-step framework, state the pattern used, and state time and space complexity. Journal your results and re-solve any incomplete problems in 3 days.

interview_war_story.story: The problem was Koko Eating Bananas. The candidate immediately said 'binary search on the answer' — a strong start. They set lo=1, hi=max(piles). Then they wrote: 'if canFinish(mid): lo=mid+1 (search for larger valid k).' WRONG direction — they were looking for MAXIMUM instead of MINIMUM. The interviewer said: 'Are you looking for the minimum or maximum feasible speed?' Candidate realised: 'Minimum — so when canFinish is true, I should try smaller values: hi=mid, not lo=mid+1.' Fixed in 30 seconds. The interviewer: 'Now explain why hi=mid and not hi=mid-1.' Candidate: 'mid might be the minimum itself. hi=mid-1 would exclude it.' Perfect answer.
interview_war_story.lesson: Binary search on answer: minimum feasible → hi=mid (try smaller). Maximum feasible → lo=mid (try larger). The direction of the binary search (left vs right on success) depends on whether you want minimum or maximum. Getting this backwards is the most common mistake.

questions.question: A problem asks: 'Find the minimum speed Koko must eat bananas to finish all piles in h hours.' This is binary search on the answer. What must be true for binary search to apply?
options: The answer must be an integer

The feasibility check must be monotonic: if speed k works, any speed k+1 also works (more speed never hurts). This monotonicity lets you binary search: is speed mid feasible? Yes→try smaller. No→try larger.
The piles must be sorted
The answer must be less than n
questions.explanation: Binary search on the answer requires monotonicity: if speed k works (finishes in <=h hours), then any speed k+1 also works. This means feasibility is a boolean function that transitions from false to true at exactly one point (the minimum feasible speed). Binary search finds that transition point.

questions.question: You have an unsorted array and need to find if any two elements sum to a target. What is the most efficient approach?
options: Sort first (O(n log n)), then two pointers O(n) — total O(n log n)
Hash map — O(n) single pass without sorting
Sort first then binary search for each element's complement — O(n log n)
Always use O(n^2) nested loops for unsorted arrays
questions.explanation: Hash map gives O(n) without sorting. But if you need to find ALL pairs (not just one), sorting + two pointers is O(n log n) + O(n) = O(n log n). If the array is already sorted, two pointers is strictly O(n). Sort-first adds O(n log n) but enables O(n) two-pointer or binary search afterward — often the better trade when multiple queries follow.

questions.question: Binary search on the answer for 'minimum k such that f(k) is true'. What is the pattern for the binary search?
options: lo=0,hi=INF; if f(mid): hi=mid; else lo=mid+1; return lo
lo=0,hi=INF; if f(mid): result=mid; lo=mid+1; else hi=mid-1; return result
lo=0,hi=INF; always halve
No fixed pattern — it depends
questions.explanation: For MINIMUM k where f(k) is true (and f is monotonic: once true, stays true for all larger k): if f(mid) is true, mid might be the answer but a smaller one might also work — go left: hi=mid. If f(mid) is false, mid is too small — go right: lo=mid+1. Loop exits at lo=hi=minimum feasible k. Return lo.

coding_quest.title: Koko Eating Bananas — Binary Search On The Answer
coding_quest.problem_statement: Koko has piles=[3,6,7,11] and h=8 hours. She can eat k bananas per hour from one pile. Find the minimum k such that she finishes all piles in <=h hours (ceil(pile/k) hours per pile). Apply the 5-step framework. The answer is a binary search on k in range [1, max(piles)].

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: A common wrong approach is binary searching with hi=mid-1 when canFinish returns true. This eliminates mid as a candidate — but mid could be the minimum. Use hi=mid (not hi=mid-1) when the check succeeds, and lo<hi for the loop condition.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(n log maxPile) but may skip the correct answer

optimal_solution.complexity: O(n log maxPile) — binary search on [1..maxPile] with O(n) check each step.

hints.text: Binary search template for MINIMUM k: lo=1, hi=max(piles). While lo<hi: mid=...; if canFinish(mid): hi=mid (mid works, try smaller). Else: lo=mid+1 (too slow). Return lo.

Why hi=mid (not mid-1): mid might be the minimum feasible speed. Using hi=mid-1 eliminates it as a candidate. Using hi=mid narrows the range while keeping mid. Why lo<hi and not lo<=hi: with hi=mid, using lo<=hi could loop forever when lo=hi.
while(lo<hi){const mid=lo+Math.floor((hi-lo)/2);if(canFinish(piles,h,mid))hi=mid;else lo=mid+1;}return lo;

theory_mcq.question: What does 'binary search on the answer' mean as an advanced pattern, and how does it differ from standard binary search on an ARRAY?
options: It's identical to standard binary search; there's no meaningful difference

Standard binary search operates on an array's INDICES, narrowing down to find a specific element's position; 'binary search on the answer' instead applies the SAME halving search strategy to a RANGE OF POSSIBLE ANSWER VALUES (not array positions), repeatedly testing whether a candidate value is FEASIBLE (using some verification function) and narrowing the value range based on that feasibility check, even when no actual sorted array is being searched at all
Binary search on the answer can only be used for sorting algorithms, never searching
This pattern only works when the answer is already known in advance
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit description: 'Binary search on the answer: applying binary search to a value range, not an array' — the maxCutLength example demonstrates this exactly: instead of searching array indices, it searches a RANGE of possible rope-cutting lengths [1, maxLength], using a feasibility check (can we get k pieces of this length?) to decide which half of the value range to continue searching.

theory_mcq.question: What recognition signals does the lesson give for identifying when an O(log n) approach (binary search in some form) is the right tool for a new problem?
options: There are no specific recognition signals; this must be guessed randomly

'sorted array', 'search', and 'find minimum/maximum in constraint' are explicitly given as the lesson's recognition signals for the O(log n) pattern — these phrases in a problem statement suggest binary search (in its standard, rotated-array, or binary-search-on-the-answer forms) is likely the appropriate technique
Only the exact phrase 'binary search' qualifies as a valid signal
O(log n) signals only apply to problems involving strings, never numbers
theory_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's exact stated recognition signals: "O(log n) recognition signal: 'sorted array', 'search', 'find minimum/maximum in constraint'" — these are the language patterns that should prompt considering a binary-search-based approach, whether on an actual array or on a range of candidate answer values.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `maxCutLength(ropes, k)` conceptually: at each step of the binary search, what does the `pieces` calculation determine, and how does the result of that calculation drive the narrowing decision?
options: pieces always equals k regardless of the candidate length

`pieces = ropes.reduce((sum, r) => sum + Math.floor(r / mid), 0)` computes the TOTAL number of pieces of length `mid` that COULD be cut across ALL the ropes combined, by summing `floor(rope_length / mid)` for each rope; if this total (`pieces`) is >= k, the candidate length `mid` is FEASIBLE (meeting the requirement), so the search tries an even LARGER candidate length (`lo = mid + 1`, while recording mid as a valid result); if `pieces < k`, mid is too large to achieve k pieces, so the search tries a SMALLER candidate length (`hi = mid - 1`)
pieces represents the number of ropes, not the number of cuttable pieces
The pieces calculation has no bearing on which direction the search narrows
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the core feasibility-check logic of binary-search-on-the-answer: for a CANDIDATE piece length (mid), summing `floor(rope_length/mid)` across all ropes gives the TOTAL pieces achievable at that length — comparing this total to the REQUIRED count k determines whether mid is achievable (search for an even better/larger feasible length) or not (search smaller), exactly matching the lesson's code: `if (pieces >= k) { result = mid; lo = mid + 1; } else { hi = mid - 1; }`.

0 problems are marked true; all entries have blind75 set to false
All 9 problems in the list are marked blind75: true

syntax_mcq.question: In `ropes.reduce((sum, r) => sum + Math.floor(r / mid), 0)`, what does the `0` as the second argument to `.reduce()` accomplish?
options: It limits the reduce operation to processing only 0 elements

It provides the INITIAL VALUE for the accumulator (`sum`) before any array elements are processed — starting the running total at 0 ensures the first rope's contribution (`Math.floor(r/mid)`) is added to a correct baseline of zero, rather than (without this argument) potentially using the array's first element itself as a starting point, which could produce wildly incorrect results for this particular calculation
It causes the reduce to always return exactly 0
It specifies the array index to start reducing from
syntax_mcq.explanation: `.reduce(callback, initialValue)` uses the provided initialValue (here, 0) as the starting point for the accumulator — this is essential for a SUM calculation, since without an explicit initial value, reduce would default to using the array's first element as the starting accumulator (which here would be a raw rope LENGTH, not a piece count), producing an incorrect total.
